title: Turner syndrome: short stature and delayed puberty
desc: This station involves taking a history from the mother of a 13-year-old girl with short stature and absent puberty, requesting and interpreting investigations for suspected Turner syndrome, and counselling the mother about the diagnosis and management plan.
stem:
You are the doctor in a General Practice clinic. The mother of a 13-year-old girl (the child) has brought her in because she is much shorter than her classmates and has not started puberty. The child is waiting outside with a nurse. The growth chart shows her height has tracked below the 3rd centile since age 4. Today she measures 138 cm and weighs 36 kg.

You have 2 minutes reading time and 8 minutes in the station.
tasks: Take a focussed history from the mother (3 minutes).
Tell the examiner the examination features you would look for and the investigations you would request, with the reason for each. Interpret the results the examiner gives you (2 minutes).
Explain the diagnosis and your management plan to the mother, including safety-netting and follow-up (3 minutes).
patient:
Profile: mother of a 13-year-old girl (the child); attends alone. GP clinic. Not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

Opening statement: 'She is much smaller than her friends and hasn't started puberty.'

History (answer only if asked):

  • Growth: shortest in class since primary school and slow growing. Height below the 3rd centile since age 4; now 138 cm, 36 kg.
  • Puberty: no breast development, no periods; a little fine pubic hair this year. Mother's periods began at 12. Mother 165 cm, father 178 cm. No family history of short stature, late puberty or early menopause.
  • Birth: term, 2.7 kg; hands and feet puffy for the first weeks.
  • Many ear infections as a toddler; now struggles to hear in noisy classrooms. A soft heart murmur was once mentioned and never followed up. One urinary infection at age 5.
  • No diarrhoea, abdominal pain, headaches, vision change, vomiting or weight loss. Mild tiredness, feels the cold. Eats well. No medications or allergies; immunisations up to date. Development normal; finds maths hard. Feels left out and embarrassed at school.

ICE: Idea: a 'late bloomer' like her father. Concern: a serious hormone problem and her confidence. Expectation: tests, and help to grow and start puberty.

Examiner findings (give when examination is requested): BP 118/64 right arm, 120/66 leg; femoral pulses present; soft ejection systolic murmur. Webbed neck, low posterior hairline, widely spaced nipples, wide carrying angle, breast Tanner stage 1, pubic hair stage 2.

Results (give when requested): Karyotype 45,X in all 30 cells counted; no Y material. FSH 58 IU/L, LH 24 IU/L (prepubertal under 5), oestradiol under 40 pmol/L. TSH 7.8 mIU/L (0.5-4.5), free T4 normal, anti-TPO positive. tTG-IgA negative, total IgA normal. Echo: bicuspid aortic valve, no coarctation, normal aortic root. Renal ultrasound: horseshoe kidney, no hydronephrosis. Audiology: mild bilateral conductive hearing loss.

Behaviour (task 3): anxious and tearful once the diagnosis is given. If not covered, ask one at a time: 'Did I cause this?' 'Could my next child have it?' 'Will she grow taller?' 'Will she go through puberty?' 'Can she have children?' 'What happens next?' Interrupt jargon: 'What does that mean?'
guide:
A high-performing candidate would take a focussed history that calculates the mid-parental height and shows the child is well below it. They would recognise the Turner features, request a 30-cell karyotype and give a reason for each test (gonadotrophins, echocardiogram, renal ultrasound, thyroid, coeliac and hearing). They would interpret the results correctly and explain the diagnosis sensitively without blame. They would outline growth hormone, oestrogen induction, fertility counselling and lifelong follow-up, and give specific safety-net advice.

A borderline candidate would suspect a chromosomal cause but give vague investigation reasons, miss the cardiac and renal screening, or not explain mosaicism. They would use jargon, rush the explanation, or leave out fertility, psychosocial support or safety-netting.
explain:
Recognition

Turner syndrome (45,X or a variant) should be considered in any girl with unexplained short stature or delayed or arrested puberty. Height below the mid-parental range, neonatal lymphoedema, recurrent otitis media, a webbed neck, low hairline, wide carrying angle and widely spaced nipples support the diagnosis.

Investigations and why

A karyotype counting at least 30 cells detects low-level mosaicism, and Y chromosome material is sought because of gonadoblastoma risk. Raised LH and FSH with low oestradiol show ovarian insufficiency. Echocardiography (with cardiac MRI per cardiology) looks for bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation and aortic dilatation, which carry a lifelong risk of dissection. Renal ultrasound looks for a horseshoe kidney. TFTs and anti-TPO, coeliac serology and audiology detect the common associated autoimmune and hearing problems.

Management

Paediatric endocrinology leads growth hormone treatment and oestrogen puberty induction. Induction is started on time and increased gradually, and it supports breast and uterine development and bone health. Fertility counselling covers premature ovarian insufficiency, donor oocytes and fertility preservation, and any pregnancy needs prior cardiac assessment. Care is lifelong, with cardiac, thyroid, hearing, bone, metabolic and psychosocial follow-up and a planned transition to adult services.

Communication

Give the news in private, in plain language, and say it is not the parents' fault. Allow time for emotion, and offer written information and support groups.
points: Consider Turner syndrome in any girl with unexplained short stature or delayed puberty; compare height with the mid-parental height.
A karyotype should count at least 30 cells to detect mosaicism, with Y material testing where indicated.
Raised LH and FSH with low oestradiol indicate ovarian insufficiency.
Screen for bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation and aortic dilatation, and for a horseshoe kidney.
Screen for thyroid disease, coeliac disease and hearing loss, and continue this lifelong.
Growth hormone and oestrogen induction are led by paediatric endocrinology; oestrogen is started at about 11-12 years and increased gradually.
refs: Gravholt CH, Andersen NH, Conway GS, et al. Clinical practice guideline for the care of girls and women with Turner syndrome: proceedings from the 2023 Aarhus International Turner Syndrome Guideline Meeting (International Turner Syndrome clinical practice guideline, Gravholt 2024). Eur J Endocrinol. 2024;190(6):G53-G151.

check.x: Handwashes, introduces self, confirms the identity of the mother and child, and explains the purpose of the consultation.
Uses sensitive, jargon-free language with appropriate eye contact, and acknowledges the mother's worry.
Takes a growth and puberty history:

kids.x: Growth: below the 3rd centile since age 4 and now 138 cm, well below the mid-parental height of 165 cm (mother 165 + father 178 − 13, divided by 2).
Puberty: no breast development or menarche at 13 years; mother's menarche at 12; no family history of short stature or delayed puberty.

check.x: Asks about Turner-associated features and excludes other causes: neonatal hand and foot swelling (lymphoedema), recurrent otitis media and hearing, murmur, urinary infections, thyroid and coeliac symptoms, chronic illness, poor nutrition, headaches or visual change.

Describes examination features: webbed neck, low posterior hairline, wide carrying angle, widely spaced nipples, lymphoedema, Tanner staging, and arm and leg blood pressure with femoral pulses (coarctation).
States the leading diagnosis is Turner syndrome with primary ovarian insufficiency.
Requests a peripheral blood karyotype counting at least 30 cells to detect low-level mosaicism, with testing for Y chromosome material if mosaic or a marker chromosome is found (gonadoblastoma risk).
Requests further investigations and gives the reason for each:

kids.x: LH, FSH and oestradiol: raised gonadotrophins with low oestradiol confirm ovarian insufficiency.
Echocardiogram (cardiac MRI per cardiology) with four-limb blood pressure: bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation and aortic root dilatation.
Renal ultrasound: horseshoe kidney and other structural anomalies, with risk of infection and obstruction.
TSH, free T4 and anti-TPO, coeliac serology (tTG-IgA with total IgA) and audiology: autoimmune thyroid disease, coeliac disease and hearing loss are common in Turner syndrome.

check.x: Interprets the results: 45,X in 30 of 30 cells confirms Turner syndrome (no mosaicism, no Y material); FSH 58 and LH 24 IU/L with oestradiol under 40 pmol/L is hypergonadotropic hypogonadism; bicuspid aortic valve without coarctation needs cardiology surveillance; horseshoe kidney without hydronephrosis; raised TSH with positive anti-TPO is autoimmune thyroiditis; coeliac screen negative; mild conductive hearing loss.

Explains the diagnosis sensitively and checks understanding: a chromosomal condition where all or some cells have one X chromosome missing; a random event, not caused by anything the parents did; recurrence risk in future pregnancies is very low; intelligence is usually normal; pauses for emotion and offers time and a second appointment.

kids.x: Urgent referral to paediatric endocrinology for growth hormone (benefit greatest if started early; may still be considered while growth plates are open) and oestrogen puberty induction (low-dose, usually transdermal, started at 11-12 years and increased gradually over 2-3 years) for breast and uterine development and bone health; dosing is set by endocrinology.

Cardiology referral; fertility counselling (most have premature ovarian insufficiency; oocyte donation and fertility preservation discussed by specialists; cardiac review before any pregnancy); psychosocial and learning support and support groups; lifelong follow-up including annual TSH and transition to an adult Turner clinic.

check.x: Gives specific safety-net advice and follow-up: urgent Emergency Department review for chest or tearing back pain, breathlessness, palpitations or fainting; prompt review for ear pain, discharge or worsening hearing, fever with flank pain or burning urine, persistent diarrhoea, abdominal pain or weight loss, or excessive thirst and urination; GP review within 2 weeks to check referrals are booked and support the family.

focus: Turner syndrome: short stature and delayed puberty in a girl
